reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A genetically diverse group of inherited disorders defined by length-dependent degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, producing progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness
Inheritance may be autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, with many causative genes designated by SPG numbers

Divided clinically into pure forms, with predominantly spastic paraparesis and bladder symptoms, and complicated forms with additional features such as ataxia, neuropathy, cognitive impairment, or retinopathy
SPG4 (spastin) is the most common autosomal dominant pure form, while SPG7 and others contribute to recessive and complicated cases
Spasticity typically dominates over weakness, so gait is stiff and scissoring, and brisk reflexes with extensor plantar responses are expected
Bladder urgency and mild reduction of vibration sense at the toes are common accompaniments in pure forms
Diagnosis requires excluding acquired myelopathies and structural cord lesions, supported by family history and gene panel testing
Management centres on spasticity control, physiotherapy, gait aids, and bladder care, as no cure exists
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary spastic paraplegia is characterised by a distal, length-dependent axonopathy that preferentially affects the longest fibres of the corticospinal tracts and, in some forms, the dorsal columns. The many implicated genes converge on cellular processes including axonal transport, mitochondrial function, myelination, and membrane trafficking, and their disruption leads to progressive degeneration of the terminal portions of long descending motor axons. This anatomy explains the predominance of lower-limb spasticity with relatively preserved upper limbs in pure forms.
additionalDifferentials: Compressive or structural spinal cord lesions
Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory myelopathies
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
Dopa-responsive dystonia and primary lateral sclerosis
Tropical spastic paraparesis and infective myelopathies
additionalInvestigations: Spinal cord and brain MRI to exclude structural and demyelinating disease
Gene panel testing for SPG and related genes
Very-long-chain fatty acids and vitamin B12 to exclude mimics
Nerve conduction studies where a complicated form with neuropathy is suspected
Cognitive, ophthalmological, or other targeted assessment in complicated forms
Detailed family history and examination of relatives
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric progression suggesting a compressive or inflammatory cause
Sensory level or sphincter failure pointing to an acquired myelopathy
Prominent bulbar or upper-limb involvement inconsistent with a pure form
Systemic features suggesting a treatable metabolic or inflammatory mimic
reference.prognosis: Pure forms are typically slowly progressive with preserved life expectancy but gradually increasing gait disability and reliance on aids; complicated forms carry more variable outcomes depending on the associated neurological features.
pitfalls: Labelling a progressive spastic paraparesis as hereditary before excluding treatable acquired causes
Overlooking the significance of subtle family history
Missing associated features that indicate a complicated subtype
Neglecting bladder and spasticity management that improve function
management: Reduce lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, focal botulinum toxin injections, and intrathecal baclofen in severe refractory cases
Maintain function and prevent contractures with physiotherapy, stretching programmes, gait and mobility aids and occupational therapy
Manage bladder urgency with antimuscarinic agents and bladder training
Provide orthopaedic input including orthoses and tendon-lengthening surgery for fixed deformity or contracture
In complicated forms, target associated features such as ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment or retinopathy
Deliver care through a multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation team
Offer genetic counselling reflecting autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive or X-linked inheritance with assessment of relatives
